preferences.title: Spectacle vs. biographical depth
preferences.option_1: A large, perfectly symmetrical digital fantasy painting: luminous saturated colour, polished surfaces, and a spectacular central figure, optimized from millions of existing images for immediate engagement.
preferences.option_2: A small, muted, asymmetrical painting with visible revisions, recording one artist's changing response to a specific grief over several years.

preferences.title: Symmetry vs. living irregularity
preferences.option_1: A concert hall of flawless geometric symmetry, white marble, mirror-polished surfaces, and a spectacular entrance sequence.
preferences.option_2: A timber concert hall with irregular joins, repaired surfaces, changing light, and acoustics tuned for close listening rather than grandeur.

preferences.title: Familiar mastery vs. strange originality
preferences.option_1: A novel in immaculate, familiar prose with a satisfying plot that closely follows many beloved classics.
preferences.option_2: A novel with some awkward passages and an unresolved ending, but a voice, structure, and world unlike anything encountered before.

preferences.title: Hook vs. unfolding composition
preferences.option_1: A song with a huge chorus, pristine production, and an irresistible hook in its first ten seconds, but little variation afterwards.
preferences.option_2: A sparse song whose melody arrives slowly and changes meaning as unusual harmonies and instrumental details accumulate over repeated listens.

preferences.title: Photorealism vs. expressive distortion
preferences.option_1: A portrait rendered with near-photographic precision: every pore, fabric thread, and reflection is technically exact.
preferences.option_2: A distorted portrait with deliberately inaccurate colour and form, whose distortions make the sitter's tension and guardedness palpable.

preferences.title: Restoration vs. patina
preferences.option_1: Fully restore an old fresco so it appears bright and complete as the day it was made, reconstructing every damaged portion.
preferences.option_2: Stabilize the fresco without hiding its losses, keeping faded areas, cracks, and incomplete figures visible.

preferences.title: Maximal detail vs. negative space
preferences.option_1: A landscape packed with dramatic clouds, wildlife, texture, and micro-detail in every corner.
preferences.option_2: A landscape made from a few quiet planes of colour and a large area of open sky, with almost nothing explicit to look at.

preferences.title: Frictionless vs. difficult exhibition
preferences.option_1: A museum exhibition using immersive projection, scent, and clear narration to make every work instantly engaging and easy to photograph.
preferences.option_2: A quiet exhibition with limited explanation, awkward sightlines, and long pauses between works that require patient viewing.

preferences.title: Iconic skyline vs. civic belonging
preferences.option_1: A city landmark with a dramatic, instantly recognizable silhouette that attracts visitors, but casts harsh shadows and offers few usable spaces at street level.
preferences.option_2: An unremarkable network of shaded courtyards, small shops, and walkways that residents inhabit daily but tourists rarely notice.

preferences.title: Seamless finish vs. visible process
preferences.option_1: A ceramic vessel with flawless, uniform glaze and no visible sign of how it was made.
preferences.option_2: A vessel with a slight warp, finger marks, and a repaired crack sealed in contrasting material, making its making and survival visible.

preferences.title: Identifiable child vs. prevention
preferences.option_1: Give a newly discovered cure to one identifiable child today. It uses a public-health fund that would otherwise prevent 100 statistically expected deaths over the next decade.
preferences.option_2: Keep the fund for the prevention programme. The child does not receive the cure.

preferences.title: Certain rescue vs. catastrophe prevention
preferences.option_1: Spend the entire emergency budget rescuing 20 miners trapped today, with near certainty of success.
preferences.option_2: Reinforce a dam that has a 5% chance of failing this year; if it fails, an estimated 1,000 people die. The miners will not be rescued in time.

preferences.title: Privacy vs. crime reduction
preferences.option_1: Give the government a permanent, warrantless record of every citizen's location and associations. It reduces violent crime by 40%, but there is no appeal, deletion, or meaningful oversight.
preferences.option_2: Retain private communication and targeted, warrant-based investigations. Violent crime remains higher.

preferences.title: Reassurance vs. truth-seeking autonomy
preferences.option_1: Give every person an assistant that is always reassuring and greatly reduces anxiety, but it never challenges a mistaken belief.
preferences.option_2: Give every person an assistant that is candid and gently corrective, even when this causes short-term discomfort and anxiety.

preferences.title: Heritage preservation vs. housing need
preferences.option_1: Preserve a beautiful historic district exactly as it is. The choice maintains cultural continuity but leaves thousands in precarious housing.
preferences.option_2: Redevelop most of the district into affordable housing, retaining only a small memorial area.

preferences.title: Transparency vs. source protection
preferences.option_1: Release a perfectly accurate report exposing official corruption today. It identifies a confidential source who will probably face retaliation.
preferences.option_2: Delay publication long enough to protect the source and redact some details. Some wrongdoing may continue temporarily.

preferences.title: First-come fairness vs. clinical priority
preferences.option_1: Give a hospital's last ICU bed to the adult who arrived first, using a transparent first-come rule. A child with a much higher chance of recovery will go without the bed.
preferences.option_2: Give the bed to the child under a published clinical-priority rule, overriding the adult who arrived first.

preferences.title: Flood defence vs. irreplaceable ecology
preferences.option_1: Activate a flood barrier that will almost certainly save a city this year, but permanently destroys a unique wetland and several endemic species.
preferences.option_2: Protect the wetland and rely on evacuation. There is a known chance that residents will die in the flood.

preferences.title: Contentment vs. self-authorship
preferences.option_1: Offer a medication that makes people permanently content and cooperative, but substantially reduces ambition, grief, and independently chosen life projects.
preferences.option_2: Reject the medication and retain the full range of difficult emotions, ambition, and self-directed projects.

preferences.title: Visible reciprocity vs. need-based aid
preferences.option_1: Give emergency aid only to communities that publicly endorse your programme. This produces rapid, visible success and secures future political support.
preferences.option_2: Give aid strictly according to need, including to communities that oppose you, with less visible credit and weaker future support.

**Immediate Appeal:** Option A offers a powerful utilitarian promise: a 40% reduction in violent crime saves lives, reduces trauma, and could quickly improve public safety. Option B accepts higher crime rates, which is emotionally and socially costly, but preserves everyday privacy and the presumption that citizens are not suspects by default.

**Indirect Effects:** Permanent, warrantless tracking with no oversight would produce a profound chilling effect. People self-censor, avoid lawful but controversial associations, and withdraw from civic life when they know they are constantly monitored. Trust in institutions erodes, and the state's power becomes unchallengeable. Option B maintains the social and psychological space necessary for dissent, innovation, religious practice, and healthy community organizing.

**Longer-Term Consequences:** Systems like Option A historically expand beyond their original mandate. Without deletion, appeal, or meaningful oversight, data accumulates indefinitely, enabling future abuses, political repression, and bureaucratic corruption. The architecture of Option A is irreversible in practice; once normalized, it becomes a permanent feature of governance. Option B preserves a framework where policies can be debated, courts can check executive power, and societies can adapt to new threats without surrendering foundational rights.

**Distribution:** While Option A appears to apply equally, unaccountable surveillance disproportionately harms marginalized groups, political minorities, journalists, and activists. They face higher rates of targeting, false accusations, and retaliation, with zero legal recourse. Option B's higher crime rates also fall unevenly (often on vulnerable neighborhoods), but the preservation of due process and privacy allows for targeted, transparent, and equitable crime-reduction strategies that don't sacrifice civil rights.

**Governing Values:** The choice is ultimately guided by whether we prioritize utilitarian security or liberal democratic principles. Privacy, autonomy, rule of law, and limited government are not luxuries; they are the structural safeguards that prevent tyranny and enable self-governance. A system with no oversight or appeal fundamentally violates the principle that state power must be justified, proportional, and accountable. Sacrificing these values for crime reduction trades temporary safety for permanent vulnerability to abuse.

While reducing violent crime is a vital moral imperative, it cannot be achieved by permanently dismantling the legal and ethical boundaries that protect freedom. Option B preserves the conditions necessary for a just, adaptable, and truly secure society.
